cards.q: What is a eukaryotic cell? Name two types of organism that have them.
cards.a: A cell whose genetic material is enclosed in a nucleus. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic.

cards.q: What does "eukaryote" mean, and why is that a useful way to remember it?
cards.a: "True nucleus". It reminds you that eukaryotic cells have their DNA inside a nucleus.

cards.q: What is a prokaryotic cell? Give an example.
cards.a: A cell with no nucleus. Its DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm. Bacteria are prokaryotes.

cards.q: List the structures found in a bacterial cell.
cards.a: Cytoplasm, cell membrane, cell wall, a single loop of DNA, and sometimes one or more plasmids.

cards.q: What is a plasmid?
cards.a: A small ring of DNA found in bacteria, in addition to the main DNA loop.

cards.q: Give two differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
cards.a: Eukaryotic: DNA in a nucleus, larger cells. Prokaryotic: DNA is a loop not in a nucleus (plus optional plasmids), much smaller cells, and a cell wall.

cards.q: Exam tip: how do you get full marks for a comparison question about eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells?
cards.a: Mention a feature of BOTH cell types in the same sentence, e.g. "bacteria have plasmids whereas animal cells do not".

cards.q: A cell is 100 µm across and a bacterium is 1 µm. How many orders of magnitude bigger is the cell?
cards.a: Two. 100 µm is 10² times 1 µm, so the cell is about 100 times larger.

cards.q: Put these in order of decreasing size: mm, nm, µm.
cards.a: mm, then µm, then nm. Each step down is ÷ 1000.

cards.q: How many micrometres (µm) are there in 1 millimetre?
What does "order of magnitude" mean?
cards.a: The nearest power of ten. Comparing two sizes by order of magnitude tells you roughly how many times bigger one is.

cards.q: What is the function of the nucleus?
cards.a: It contains the genetic material (chromosomes made of DNA) and controls the activities of the cell.

cards.q: What is the function of the cell membrane?
cards.a: It controls what moves into and out of the cell.

cards.q: What happens in mitochondria?
cards.a: Aerobic respiration, which releases energy for the cell.

cards.q: Why do muscle cells have a lot of mitochondria?
cards.a: They need to release a lot of energy by respiration so that they can contract.

cards.q: What do chloroplasts contain and what do they do?
cards.a: Chlorophyll. They absorb light energy for photosynthesis.

cards.q: Why are plasmids useful to bacteria?
cards.a: They carry extra genes (for example for antibiotic resistance) and can be passed between bacteria.

cards.q: What is the function of the cytoplasm?
cards.a: It is where most chemical reactions in the cell take place. It is a gel-like fluid containing enzymes.

cards.q: What do ribosomes do?
cards.a: They are where proteins are made (protein synthesis).

cards.q: Which three parts do plant cells often have that animal cells do not?
cards.a: Chloroplasts, a permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, and a cellulose cell wall.

cards.q: Why do some plant cells, such as root cells, not have chloroplasts?
cards.a: They are underground and get no light, so they cannot photosynthesise. That is why the spec says plant cells "often" have chloroplasts.

cards.q: What is the difference between the cell wall and the cell membrane?
cards.a: The cell wall (cellulose, outside the membrane) strengthens the cell. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.

cards.q: A sperm cell has a tail and many mitochondria. Explain how each helps it do its job.
cards.a: The tail lets it swim to the egg. The mitochondria release the energy needed for swimming.

cards.q: Why do root hair cells have long extensions?
cards.a: To give a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.

cards.q: Name the three specialised animal cells and the three specialised plant cells named in the specification.
cards.a: Animal: sperm, nerve, muscle. Plant: root hair, xylem, phloem.

cards.q: How is a nerve cell adapted for carrying electrical impulses?
cards.a: It has a long axon to carry impulses over a distance and dendrites to connect to other nerve cells.

cards.q: What is the difference between differentiation and a specialised cell?
cards.a: Differentiation is the process. A specialised cell is the result: a cell that has gained the structures it needs for a particular job.

cards.q: Why is cell differentiation important in a multicellular organism?
cards.a: It produces different cell types, each suited to a different job. These form tissues and organs and make the organism work efficiently.

cards.q: When do animal cells and plant cells differentiate?
cards.a: Most animal cells differentiate early, while the animal develops. Many plant cells can differentiate throughout life.

cards.q: In a mature animal, what is cell division mainly used for?
cards.a: Repair and replacement of cells.

cards.q: Give two advantages of an electron microscope over a light microscope.
cards.a: Higher magnification and higher resolving power, so finer detail and more sub-cellular structures can be seen.

cards.q: What is resolution (resolving power)?
cards.a: The ability to see two points that are close together as separate. Higher resolution gives a sharper, more detailed image.

cards.q: What is the magnification equation?
cards.a: Magnification = image size ÷ real size.

cards.q: An image is 12 mm long and the magnification is ×400. What is the real size, in µm?
What is the most common mistake in magnification calculations?
cards.a: Mixing units. Convert image size and real size to the same unit first (1 mm = 1000 µm).

cards.q: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria are there after 2 hours?
cards.a: 2 hours = 6 divisions, so 2⁶ = 64 bacteria.

cards.q: What is a colony of bacteria?
cards.a: A visible mass of bacteria that have all descended from one original cell by repeated binary fission.

cards.q: Why must an inoculating loop be passed through a flame before use?
cards.a: To sterilise it by killing any microorganisms on the loop, so only the intended bacteria are transferred.

cards.q: Why is the lid of a Petri dish taped on and the dish stored upside down?
cards.a: Tape stops microorganisms from the air getting in. Upside down stops condensation dripping onto the culture.

cards.q: Why are school cultures incubated at about 25 °C and not 37 °C?
cards.a: At 25 °C, human pathogens (which grow best at body temperature) are less likely to grow.

cards.q: A clear zone around an antibiotic disc has a diameter of 14 mm. What is its area?
cards.a: r = 7 mm, so area = π × 7² ≈ 154 mm².

cards.q: State the relative charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
cards.a: Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1.

cards.q: Why is an atom electrically neutral?
cards.a: It has the same number of protons (positive) as electrons (negative), so the charges cancel.

cards.q: What is the atomic number?
cards.a: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom. It identifies the element.

cards.q: What is the mass number?
cards.a: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

cards.q: What are isotopes?
cards.a: Atoms of the same element (same number of protons) with different numbers of neutrons.

cards.q: What are the relative masses of a proton, a neutron and an electron?
cards.a: Proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small (almost zero).

cards.q: Where is most of the mass of an atom?
cards.a: In the nucleus, because protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons.

cards.q: What is the approximate radius of an atom, and how does the nucleus compare?
cards.a: About 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m). The nucleus has a radius about 1/10 000 of the atom.

cards.q: An atom of sodium is written ²³₁₁Na. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it have?
cards.a: 11 protons, 12 neutrons (23 − 11), and 11 electrons (neutral atom).

cards.q: Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Calculate its relative atomic mass.
Why is relative atomic mass often not a whole number?
cards.a: It is an average of the masses of an element's isotopes, taking account of how much of each there is.

cards.q: Which energy level do electrons fill first?
cards.a: The lowest available energy level (the shell closest to the nucleus).

cards.q: Write the electronic structure of magnesium (atomic number 12) and chlorine (17).
cards.a: Magnesium 2,8,2. Chlorine 2,8,7.

cards.q: Describe the plum pudding model of the atom.
cards.a: A ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

cards.q: What did the alpha particle scattering experiment show, and what did that lead to?
cards.a: Most alpha particles passed straight through, a few were deflected and a very few bounced back. So the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus, which replaced the plum pudding model.

cards.q: How did Bohr adapt the nuclear model?
cards.a: He proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances, in shells (energy levels).

cards.q: What is needed for charge to flow round a closed circuit?
cards.a: A source of potential difference, such as a cell or battery.

cards.q: What is electric current?
cards.a: The rate of flow of electric charge.

cards.q: Write the charge flow equation with units.
cards.a: Charge flow (C) = current (A) × time (s), or Q = I t.

cards.q: A current of 2 A flows for 30 s. How much charge flows?
A current of 0.5 A flows for 2 minutes. How much charge flows?
In a series circuit, how does the current at different points compare?
cards.a: It is the same at every point in a single closed loop.

cards.q: Write the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
cards.a: Potential difference (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω), or V = I R.

cards.q: A 12 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor. What is the current?
A component has 6 V across it and carries 0.5 A. What is its resistance?
For a given potential difference, what happens to the current if the resistance increases?
cards.a: The current decreases, because current = potential difference ÷ resistance.

cards.q: What is an ohmic conductor? Describe its I–V graph.
cards.a: A resistor whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature. The graph is a straight line through the origin.

cards.q: What happens to the resistance of a filament lamp as it gets hotter?
cards.a: It increases, so the I–V graph curves (current rises less steeply).

cards.q: How does a diode behave?
cards.a: Current flows in one direction only. In the other direction its resistance is very high.

cards.q: How does the resistance of a thermistor change with temperature?
cards.a: It decreases as temperature increases.

cards.q: How does the resistance of an LDR change with light?
cards.a: It decreases as light intensity increases.
